title: Sebastian and the Well
premise: Tamsin Ravensworth returns to the family farmhouse to bury their twin Sebastian, who drowned in the old well at seven—except Tamsin has always suspected it was themselves who died, and the surviving twin is a lie they've told for thirty years. Setting up sleep cameras to document the nocturnal noises, Tamsin captures a second voice answering questions in Sebastian's cadence, asking to finish the song their mother sang before she vanished. As Tamsin pieces together that their mother traded one twin to the well and the village has been singing the debt forward ever since, they must learn the song's final verse—which can only be heard by standing at the well's mouth at night. In the climax, Tamsin chooses love over duty: instead of offering themselves or another as the verse demands, they sing the song backward, unmaking the bargain, freeing Sebastian's voice but erasing every memory anyone holds of him. The book ends with Tamsin alone in an empty house, grieving a brother no record confirms existed, keeping his memory alive as the only loyal witness left.
about_author: Petra Ashgrove is the pen name of a former rural archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records of disappearances across the English moors. Their fiction blends folk horror with quiet domestic grief, and 'Sebastian and the Well' is their third novel.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They arrive at Ravensworth Farm for Sebastian's funeral, fifteen years after leaving, and notice the coffin is sealed and the dates on the death certificate don't align with their own memories. Emotional beat: disorientation masked as grief, the first crack in the story Tamsin tells themselves.

chapters.title: Housekeeping for the Dead
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Clearing Sebastian's room, they find childhood drawings of two children by a well—one drawn in pencil that stops mid-stroke—and a cassette labeled 'for when you remember.' Emotional beat: dread braided with tenderness; the house resists being tidied.

chapters.title: Noises Have Explanations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. First night home: pipes knock, floorboards sigh, and Tamsin narrates rational causes aloud like a ritual. A neighbor, Mrs. Callow, warns them not to answer if something calls their name. Emotional beat: brittle self-soothing beginning to fail.

chapters.title: The Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They set up a recorder out of insomnia-driven curiosity. Playback reveals Tamsin talking in their sleep—and a second voice, low and patient, answering questions Tamsin doesn't remember asking. Emotional beat: vertigo; the rational framework collapses.

chapters.title: Questions at Night
chapters.summary: Alternating transcript excerpts and Tamsin's waking commentary. The second voice knows shared childhood secrets only Sebastian could know, including the song their mother sang. It asks Tamsin to come to the well. Emotional beat: longing warring with terror—the voice sounds like home.

chapters.title: Mrs. Callow's Version
chapters.summary: Mrs. Callow's POV. The elderly neighbor recalls the night the twins were born and the night their mother walked into the fields singing, and how the village has always 'paid the well its due.' She refuses to say more. Emotional beat: complicit silence; loyalty to tradition over truth.

chapters.title: What the Parish Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, investigating church and county archives. Records show a Ravensworth child drowned in 1994—but the name is smudged, and the register lists twins born, one baptized, one 'commended.' Emotional beat: the past is deliberately illegible; someone edited history.

chapters.title: The Cassette
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They play the tape from Sebastian's room: their mother's voice teaching two children a counting-song, then her voice alone, reciting a verse neither child was allowed to learn. The tape ends with water sounds. Emotional beat: heartbreak; motherhood revealed as negotiation.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, flashback chapter. How they left at eighteen, built a city life, never slept without white noise, never loved anyone long enough to share a bed through the night. Emotional beat: recognition that the whole adult life was avoidance.

chapters.title: The Well in Daylight
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They visit the capped well at noon, armed with daylight and a flashlight, and find fresh flowers on the stones—someone still tends it. Carved inside the cap: two names, both theirs. Emotional beat: confrontation with the physical anchor of the haunting.

chapters.title: Second Voice, First Name
chapters.summary: Night recordings escalate. The voice uses Tamsin's childhood nickname and describes the drowning from underwater—not accusing, just remembering. Tamsin answers aloud for the first time. Emotional beat: intimacy with the impossible; guilt turning into conversation.

chapters.title: The Village Choir
chapters.summary: Tamsin attends the harvest service and realizes the congregation sings the mother's counting-song as a hymn, minus the last verse, which the hymnal omits. The vicar goes pale when Tamsin hums it. Emotional beat: communal complicity; the town is the haunting's chorus.

chapters.title: Duty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Vicar Ellery's POV. He explains—or half-explains—the arrangement: every generation, the well takes a Ravensworth unless the family keeps the song unfinished and the debt ambiguous. His own grandfather helped write the hymnal. Emotional beat: duty dressed as mercy; institutional cowardice.

chapters.title: Sebastian Remembers Drowning
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The voice recounts the full night: mother singing, one child lowered, one hidden, and the moment the wrong twin screamed the right name. Tamsin's memories begin surfacing in dreams they can't dismiss. Emotional beat: devastating clarity; identity itself becomes unstable.

chapters.title: Am I the One Who Died?
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, interior crisis. Evidence mounts that Tamsin died and 'Sebastian' lived under the wrong name for eight years before the well reclaimed what it was owed. The recordings now answer questions Tamsin hasn't asked yet. Emotional beat: existential unraveling; grief for oneself.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Piecing together fragments—cassette, Mrs. Callow's humming, the voice's whispers—they reconstruct the final verse, which promises the well will 'sleep forever' if sung complete by a willing Ravensworth. Emotional beat: terrible empowerment; knowledge as trap.

chapters.title: Mrs. Callow's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Callow's POV. She reveals she was the mother's friend and helped hide the surviving twin, and that the mother didn't vanish—she went down the well herself to buy the children time. Her loyalty kept the lie alive out of love. Emotional beat: compassion for complicity; love and lies entangled.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The voice makes its request plain: come to the well, sing the last verse, and take Sebastian's place—or refuse, and the well starts taking villagers instead, starting with Mrs. Callow. Time is short; the water is rising elsewhere. Emotional beat: ultimatum; duty versus love made literal.

chapters.title: Night at the Well's Mouth
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax part one. At midnight they kneel at the well and hear the whole song rising from below, and understand the verse isn't a sacrifice formula—it's a contract, and contracts can be broken. Emotional beat: resolve crystallizing from despair.

chapters.title: Sung Backward
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. Instead of completing the song, Tamsin sings it in reverse, verse by verse, unbinding the bargain while the well fights back with every memory they have of Sebastian. They hold the last note until the water goes silent and the second voice says goodbye. Emotional beat: sacrificial defiance; love refusing the terms.

chapters.title: The Empty House
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, aftermath. The farm is clean, quiet, ordinary. Every photo, record, and memory others hold of Sebastian is gone—only Tamsin remembers, and the memories are already thinning at the edges. Emotional beat: hollow victory; freedom purchased with erasure.

chapters.title: Keeping the Song
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, coda. They stay at the farm, writing everything down before it fades, teaching themselves the first verses so someone will know a boy named Sebastian existed. On quiet nights, the well makes no sound at all—and Tamsin chooses to believe that means he's finally sleeping. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; loyalty outlasting truth.
